headline: Green Thumb grows sales 11% as Trulieve shrinks to a medical core
dek: Green Thumb posted $324.4 million in third-quarter revenue on Minnesota sales; Trulieve reported $230 million after deconsolidating Harvest's adult-use stores.
key_points: Green Thumb's third-quarter revenue rose 11.3% to $324.4 million and same-store sales grew 3% for the first time since late 2024, but it posted a $4.8 million GAAP loss.
Trulieve's revenue fell 20% to $230 million because the quarter covers only its medical business, while gross margin rose to 64% and net income turned slightly positive.
Both companies say DEA registrations for medical dispensaries have started arriving; Trulieve's CEO credits rescheduling with ending 280E for its medical operations.
Green Thumb guided to flat or slightly lower revenue in the fourth quarter as price compression continues.
body: Two of the largest U.S. cannabis operators reported third-quarter results this week that show how differently rescheduling is playing out across the industry. Green Thumb Industries, a mixed adult-use and medical operator, grew revenue 11.3% to $324.4 million on the back of Minnesota's new adult-use market. Trulieve, which has reshaped itself into a medical-focused company, reported $230 million in revenue, down 20% from a year earlier, but with fatter margins and positive net income.

The contrast is structural, not just operational. Trulieve's third quarter is the first full period to include only its medical operations after it deconsolidated Harvest's mixed medical and adult-use business on 3 June. Green Thumb runs both kinds of business and remains exposed to the price pressure that adult-use markets bring.
## Green Thumb: growth returns, margins slip

Green Thumb said on 4 November that Minnesota, where adult-use sales began on 17 September 2025, drove most of the increase, alongside Florida, New Jersey, New York, Ohio and Virginia and stores opened or bought over the past year. Retail revenue rose 10.1% and consumer packaged goods revenue rose 16.0%. Comparable sales at 108 stores open at least a year grew 3.0%, the first increase since the third quarter of 2024, after a decline of about 1% in the second quarter.

Profitability moved the other way on a reported basis. Gross margin fell to 45.2% from 49.4%, which the company tied to price compression and competition in some markets. It recorded a GAAP net loss of $4.8 million, or $0.02 a share, against net income of $23.3 million a year earlier, when it booked a gain on the sale of intellectual property. Normalized EBITDA, which excludes $15.8 million of licensing fees and $10.4 million of stock compensation among other items, rose to $89.4 million, or 27.6% of revenue.

Cash flow from operations was $58.3 million and the company ended the quarter with $316.0 million in cash. It added six RISE dispensaries: Port Charlotte and Port St. Lucie in Florida, Sparks in Nevada, and Hanover, West Mifflin and Allentown in Pennsylvania. On the earnings call, management said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to be flat to slightly down from the third quarter.

Management also said some of its medical licenses in Florida and Virginia are now registered with the DEA, with others pending, and noted that more than 75% of Massachusetts voters rejected Question 8, the measure to repeal the state's adult-use program, where it also operates.
> The medical-only operators are getting the tax break first. The mixed operators are getting the volume. Investors will have to decide which is worth more.
## Trulieve: a smaller, more profitable company

Trulieve's 5 November release shows the effect of becoming a medical company. Revenue of $230 million compared with $288 million a year earlier and $271 million in the second quarter. Gross margin climbed to 64% from 59%, and 95% of revenue came from its own stores. Net income attributable to shareholders was $1 million, against a $27 million loss a year earlier; adjusted EBITDA was $89 million, or 39% of revenue.

Cash generation is the headline Trulieve wants investors to see. Operating cash flow was $74 million in the quarter and $183 million over nine months, with free cash flow of $120 million year to date. It ended September with $327 million in cash and has since repaid $65 million of mortgage notes due in 2028. The company runs 208 dispensaries and said traffic in Georgia rose sevenfold after that state expanded its medical program on 1 July.

The year to date still carries heavy charges. Trulieve reported a nine-month net loss of $403 million, driven by a second-quarter loss of $406 million tied to impairments and disposals around the Harvest deconsolidation. Its balance sheet also lists $625.4 million of uncertain tax position liabilities, which reflects the long dispute over Section 280E.

Chief executive Kim Rivers credited rescheduling with unlocking DEA registration, the removal of 280E and the company's move to the New York Stock Exchange, where it now trades as TRLV after redomiciling to Delaware. Formal IRS guidance on how medical operators claim the tax change has not yet been published, as we reported on 6 November.

Other results this week point the same way. Aurora Cannabis, which Organigram agreed to buy this week in a deal Curaleaf is contesting, reported quarterly net revenue of C$86 million and a net loss of C$21.1 million, according to Marijuana Moment. The common thread is price pressure in adult-use markets and a premium on businesses that sit inside the new federal medical framework.

For Green Thumb, the fourth-quarter guide and whether comparable-store growth holds, plus any progress toward adult-use legalization in Pennsylvania, where it is adding stores. For Trulieve, the pace of Georgia and Texas expansion, the size of any 280E refunds once IRS guidance lands, and whether the uncertain tax liabilities begin to shrink. For both, the late-November deadline for DEA-registered businesses to source only from registered or applied suppliers.
